content.content:
=== P-7
POSITIONS.md:7
- P-7 **The goal is to finish what the designers intended, measured by one program, microGPT, compiled to JVM bytecode and running fast.** What the designers intended is judged by the specification in `Specification/`: the team's Working Draft of February 2011, as the revival revises it, with the Types chapter of the team's 2012 restart cited beside it (P-25). The revival revises the specification to reconcile contradictions: where the team's later work, in the compiler or in the papers on types, contradicts the original text, the text is updated to follow that work (P-26: the type group's later word wins). The language is not redesigned. The specification is a living document that states each change that the revival makes (P-95 says how a change is recorded). A pure-Java microGPT is the baseline that compiled microGPT is measured against: the optimal result, the one to aim at.

=== P-27
POSITIONS.md:25
- P-27 **The library's own practice is the standard.** What microGPT invented goes into the standard library, in the library's own style. Whoever extends the library first studies how it does the same kind of thing, and follows that pattern; exclusion, for one, is all over it. He had to find the diagonal's override himself (P-88) because that study was skipped. No fix is designed from the specification alone or from a workaround on the user's side.

=== P-146
POSITIONS.md:59
- P-146 **In a self-typed trait, the compiled checker types `self` in the method bodies as also being the implementing type.** A self-typed trait is a trait `C[\X\]` whose parameter `X` extends `C[\X\]`, such as `Integral[\I extends Integral[\I\]\]`. In its method bodies, `self` has the type `C[\X\] & X`. The method signatures keep the plain trait type, because the proofs of the POPL 2019 paper on multiple dispatch (Park, Hong, Steele and Ryu) assume that no declared type holds a type parameter inside an intersection. Only the overloading check's exclusion test reads `self` in a signature as `C[\X\] & X` (P-157). The checker refuses a type that extends such a trait at another type, since an extender must be a subtype of the static argument that it gives: `object Bad extends Integral[\ZZ32\]` is refused, because `Bad` is not a `ZZ32`. Scala has the same rule for self types. The library's text gains no self type and no `comprises` clause, and walk is unchanged. The rule accepts every self-typed method body of the library except `Integral`'s `numerator`, which each integer type declares instead. Why: the checker reads the library as the team wrote it, as P-44 does for the closure of `AnyIntegral`, by one rule that peer languages share. F-225 states the rule as built.

=== P-153
POSITIONS.md:88
- P-153 **The integer power splits on the base: an integer base gives an integer or raises an error, and a float or rational base gives the fraction.** Each integer type's `^` returns its own type at every exponent. At a negative exponent, the bases 1 and -1 give their exact power, a base of 0 raises `DivisionByZero`, and any other base raises `IntegerOverflow`. A program that wants a fraction writes a float or rational base, as in `2.0^(-1)`. Why: the team's later code gives an integer power the type of its integer base at a signed exponent (P-26, the team's later work outweighs the specification's early text). Overloads choose by type, and no type tells a negative exponent from a non-negative one, since a signed integer or a numeral can be either. So the split is on the base, and the sign of the exponent is tested at run time, as the library tests a value's sign everywhere (P-80, run-time sign tests in place of sign-refined types). Row 441: the same rule on the compiled path, whose own powers give 0 at a negative exponent and a raw Java exception at a base of 0, and overflow silently or with a raw Java exception (row 523).

=== P-154
POSITIONS.md:65
- P-154 **A list is ordered only where its element type is totally ordered.** The library's `List` extends its lexicographic order only where its element type extends `StandardTotalOrder` (conditional extension, P-151). Floats and `QQ` are only partially ordered, since NaN, and `QQ`'s 0/0, compare with nothing. So on the compiled checker a list of floats or of `QQ` has no order: no `<`, `CMP` or the other comparisons, though its `=` stays. A pair of floats stays ordered: the curator accepted that mismatch as a cost of the list rule. The tuples' own rule is not decided here. No lexicographic trait over partially ordered elements is added now: the team never wrote one, and the case touches neither the distance to the switch-over nor microGPT. Why: the team's later code bounds the element of both of its lexicographic traits by a total order (`Library/incomplete/advanced/Fortress.PartialTotalOrders.fss:117-140`; P-26, the team's later word outweighs its early text), and conditional extension is a `where` form that the team wrote (P-151). Row 774: walk's half, since walk still gives every list an order.

=== P-12
POSITIONS.md:12
- P-12 **After the switch-over, walk runs the compiled type checker on its programs, and then uses the static coercions that the checker inserts.** The curator wants the checker usable on the programs that walk runs. Today `fortress typecheck` checks a program only against the compiler's prelude, so it is no check of walk's programs (F-9 holds this fact). Walk is not changed for this before the switch-over. After it, walk runs the checker on its programs and so gains their static types. Walk then uses the static coercions that the checker inserts, in place of its choice on the run-time value (P-59, walk's choice of coercions until the switch-over).

=== P-17
POSITIONS.md:16
- P-17 **Unboxed doubles and arrays of unboxed doubles are required: without them the revival misses its point.** Why: a language meant for high performance cannot box its numbers. Today the code generator boxes every number: an `RR64` value is an object of the class `FRR64`. In Java models of microGPT's three array kernels, the dot product, the matrix product and the row lift, boxing is the main cost (F-11 holds the measurement). How arrays store doubles, as `double[]`, is P-84's decision.

content.content:
=== P-33
POSITIONS.md:30
- P-33 **The work toward microGPT compiled follows the phases, in the order that the curator approved.** These phases are steps of the work, not the compiler's phases, and they are numbered 3 to 6, after two earlier ones. Phase 3, the compiled checker reports no error on the interpreter's whole library (the distance to the switch-over at zero; F-53 defines it and holds its value); phase 4, the switch-over, first the natives, the library's `builtinPrimitive` bindings made to run on the compiled path, then the compiled path reads the interpreter's library and the compiler's prelude is deleted; phase 5, microGPT compiles: its static types, the array design and the code generator's open gaps; phase 6, microGPT runs fast. Code-generator work goes on beside that order, under either library (P-37). Row 320, an api implemented by a component of another name does not link, is part of the switch-over's design.

=== P-42
POSITIONS.md:39
- P-42 **A type parameter declared without a bound has the implicit bound `Any`, not `Object`.** `Any` holds tuples, functions and `()`, which `Object` does not. The library instantiates its generic containers at tuple types: its arrays indexed by pairs, such as `(ZZ32,ZZ32)`, are among them. The specification states the bound `Any`, with a callout that records that the Working Draft of February 2011 said `Object`. The compiled path departs from it until the switch-over, which ends the departure: while it uses the compiler's prelude, it bounds such a parameter by `Object`, and so refuses a generic instantiated at a tuple (row 412).

=== P-58
POSITIONS.md:55
- P-58 **Every native binding is a `builtinPrimitive` call naming a static helper.** A native binding is a library body that is exactly `builtinPrimitive("…")`, the library's own form, and it keeps that form. Its string is to name a static Java method in `nativeHelpers/`, the compiled path's helpers, such as `"com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleIntArith.intLT"`, in place of a glue class of walk, which the compiled path cannot use (F-32). Walk is to load the named helper through a loader beside its glue classes. At the parse, before the checker, the compiled path is to rewrite each such body into a synthetic `import java` of the helper and a call, and to refuse a string that names no helper. The bindings move onto helpers step by step, and from the step that moves a binding, the compiled checker checks it against the helper's Java signature, not all at once at the switch-over. The other form, `import java` declarations written in the library itself, is not taken. Every binding still names a glue class. Row 796: walk loads a binding's string only as a glue class. Row 309: the compiled path has no counterpart of `builtinPrimitive`.

=== P-59
POSITIONS.md:56
- P-59 **Walk chooses a coercion by the run-time value until it runs the checker, after the switch-over.** Walk has no static types. So where a coercion is needed, walk chooses it by the value's run-time type. The specification and the compiled path choose it by the static type. The curator accepts this as the interpreter's limit, and walk is not changed for it before the switch-over. A callout in the coercion chapter (`Specification/basic/conversions-coercions.tex`) states the limit. Two expected-failure tests record it: `XXXCoercionStaticRungC`, the chapter's own printed example, and `XXXCoercionStaticNarrowRungC`. After the switch-over, once walk runs the checker on its programs (P-12 orders the two steps), it uses the static coercions that the checker inserts. MicroGPT's static types are concrete, each the type of the value itself and not a trait above it, so on microGPT walk's choice and the static choice agree.

=== P-84
POSITIONS.md:92
- P-84 **An `RR64` array is stored as a Java `double[]`, unboxed, and arrays keep the team's `nat` sizes in their types.** Why: a high-performance language cannot box its array elements, and the sizes are central to the team's design. So the storage and the sizes are one design: the sizes stay in the array types as `nat` static parameters, as the library's `Vector` and `Matrix` declare them, and the compiled checker checks them. The sizes do not wait while a first version of the store carries them only as run-time fields; that layered plan was rejected. Both halves follow the library's own patterns (P-27, the library's own practice is the standard). The compiled checker checks `nat` static parameters (F-67). The compiled path's `double[]` store waits with the other array decisions until after the switch-over; among them is decision A, how an `RR64` array made through the library's generic array traits gets that store (P-85).

=== P-85
POSITIONS.md:93
- P-85 **The array design's three questions are open, with no default, and return after the switch-over with the array decisions A, B and D.** The array design is the compiled path's design for arrays. The three questions: whether the array factory chooses a store for each element type; whether the store also keeps the size as a field, beside the size in the type; and whether a factory for a size known only at run time returns the unsized `Array[\E,I\]`, whose type holds no size. These questions are apart from decisions A, B and D: decision A is how an `RR64` array made through the library's generic array traits gets the `double[]` store (P-84), B is where unboxed arithmetic happens, and D is the sizes in the model's own types (P-87). The whole preparation for the array work is to be done before the switch-over; only the work itself waits.

=== P-155
POSITIONS.md:66
- P-155 **The compiled checker checks the overloads of symbolic operators before the switch-over.** Today its overloading check reads an operator only if its name is a word of capitals, such as `MAX`, so `+`, `^`, `||`, the subscripts and the other symbolic operators pass unchecked. The check must read them by the rules that it applies to any function, so that the distance to the switch-over reaches zero with them checked. Why: the skip is a gap that the team knew, not a rule: the specification's appendix of proposed features calls the library's two subscript operators "not really a valid overloading" (`Specification/appendices/future.tex:186-207`, its item on array indexing). A zero with them unchecked would hide known errors. Each design that the check needs is brought to the curator before its rung, with the probe's measurement (`perf-probes/symbolic-operators-2/REPORT.md`); the two it found are decided: P-156, the subscripts' index bound, and P-157, vectors that stay additive groups by a change to the checker's exclusion test. Row 584: the check and its rungs.

# The corrections run

Scope: the 18 entries of `explorations/reviews/foundations/evidence/salvage-findings.md`. The exit judgement's six entries are not in it. The tool is the clarity workflow with the three additions of `brief-additions.md` beside this note, applied to its files. Commit the run's folder before the launch.

definition.name: mcp__ccd_session__dismiss_task
definition.description:
Withdraw a task suggestion you queued earlier with spawn_task.

Call this when a suggestion has gone stale: the issue was fixed in this session (by you or the user), it turned out not to be a problem after all, or you have queued a better-scoped replacement — in that case queue the replacement with spawn_task first, then dismiss the old task_id.

Only a suggestion the user hasn't acted on can be withdrawn. If they already started or dismissed it, the result says so and nothing changes; that answer is final, so don't retry or re-flag it.

reason.description: Optional short note on why the suggestion is no longer needed, e.g. "fixed in this session" or "superseded by task_ab12cd34". It doesn't change the outcome.

task_id.description: The task_id from the spawn_task result that queued the suggestion (of the form task_1a2b3c4d).

definition.name: mcp__ccd_session__spawn_task
definition.description:
Suggest a separate task for something you noticed that is outside the scope of your current work.

Call this when you come across something that deserves fixing but doesn't belong in this change — dead code, stale docs, a missing test, a confirmed TODO, a bug or security issue spotted in passing. Don't use it for trivial fixes you can make inline, for anything the user asked you to do, for vague code-smell impressions or unverified hunches, or to split off parts of your own task. The call only queues a suggestion and returns; carry on with your current work.

The user sees a "Suggested task" card in the Claude desktop app with your title and tldr, can open the full prompt, and with one click starts it as a new session — on their machine in their local clone of this repository (optionally a fresh worktree of it), or in the cloud — sends it to this session, or dismisses it. A new session starts from your prompt alone, on a checkout that may not have this session's changes, so the prompt has to stand alone: what to change and why, the files involved by repository-relative path, and any context from this conversation it depends on. Absolute paths and other state of this environment may not exist there. If the find involves a secret or credential, say where it is rather than copying the value, since the prompt is stored and displayed.

The result carries a task_id; if the suggestion later becomes moot, withdraw it with dismiss_task.

prompt.description: The opening message of the new session: the goal, the files involved by repository-relative path, the context it needs from this conversation, and what done looks like. The user can read it in full before starting; markdown is fine. Keep it to what the task needs (hard limit 32000 characters) — the new session can read the code itself.

title.description: The card's heading and the new session's title: a short imperative phrase starting with a verb, under 60 characters, that makes sense on its own — e.g. "Fix stale README badge", "Remove dead config option".

tldr.description: One or two plain sentences on what the task would do and why it is worth doing. Shown on the card under the title; it is what the user reads when deciding whether to start it, so no file paths or code.

Value objects with the same type, environment and fields
are indistinguishable.
Thus, an implementation may freely copy value objects.
Most objects with simple standard types,
such as booleans,
numeric literals,
IEEE floating-point numbers,
and integers are value objects.
---
If \VAR{T} is not a value type, then \EXP{\TYP{LinearSequence}\llbracket{}T,n\rrbracket} describes a
sequence of references, and a variable of type \EXP{\TYP{LinearSequence}\llbracket{}T,n\rrbracket} occupies
an amount of storage equal to \VAR{n} times the amount of storage required to hold
a reference.  If \VAR{T} is a value type, then \EXP{\TYP{LinearSequence}\llbracket{}T,n\rrbracket}
describes a sequence of ``unboxed'' values,
and a variable of type \EXP{\TYP{LinearSequence}\llbracket{}T,n\rrbracket} occupies an amount of storage equal
to \VAR{n} times the amount of storage required to hold one value of type \VAR{T}.

P-158Abstract members of an api

The new text

P-158 A member that an api writes abstract is declared in the component that exports the api. The component's trait or object declares each such member at the api's header, with a body or without one. The compiled export check refuses a component that leaves one out, and the checker then checks that each object defines it. Why: the compiler's prelude, the team's later work, restates each such member in the component without a body, and from March 2009 the team's export check refused a component trait that left out a member of its api's trait (edb516dba, Sukyoung Ryu); by P-26, on the team's later word, that way wins over the interpreter's library, written earlier for walk, which leaves some out. The specification's export rule does not ask for this declaration: it asks the component to declare each field and each non-abstract method of the api's trait or object, and allows a concrete declaration of an abstract one (Specification/basic/components/source-code.tex, "Export Statements"). Without the declaration, a compiled client's call of the member dies with NoSuchMethodError (row 816).

# Review-queue items, chunk p

No entry of this chunk is held. Six questions for the curator are new; number them when they go into `coordinator/review-queue.md`. Four more are already in the queue as items 215, 219, 220 and 280. They are not added again, and the notes at the end say what this pass changes in them and in item 241. Paths are under `explorations/`.

**When does a design of the compiler's prelude bind the one library (P-37)?** P-37 says that the decision settles which files survive, not the designs inside them: "the one library may take a design of the prelude's, as it took the prelude's flat shape of the number types." It gives no rule for when a design binds. On 2026-10-26 at 07:30 UTC he asked a related question: where the two libraries differed, did the revival take the prelude's deliberate later designs into the one library, or only make the checker accept what the interpreter's library wrote? The foundations judgement proposes a rule. A design of the prelude binds when the team's later word on the language backs it. It also binds when the team's text is unclear and the team's own checker enforced the design as a rule. A design that the team called temporary, or that works around a checker gap, does not bind. "Later" is a date: a 2009 line of code is not later than a 2011 paper. The rule is the judge's reasoning, not his words, so the clarity pass kept the sentence as it is. Add the rule to P-37?
   - Landed: The sentence as P-37 reads. Default: no rule, until he answers.
   - The other way: P-37 states the judgement's rule in place of the bare permission.
   - Its cost: One or two sentences of P-37. No code changes. Without a rule, each design of the prelude is weighed on its own, as P-43's flat numbers and P-158's export check were.
   - Home: POSITIONS P-37; `reviews/foundations/judgement.md`, section 3; `reviews/foundations/prelude-lens.md`, which sorts the prelude's choices into designs and stubs; `reviews/foundations/evidence/salvage-findings.md`, P-37 (b); `reviews/foundations/evidence/corrections/p/proposals.md`, "P-37", question 1
   - Needed by: before the switch-over; the prelude's three files are deleted then, and the rule says which of their designs the one library takes.

**Is `CompilerSystem` deleted at the switch-over with the compiler's prelude (P-37)?** `Library/CompilerSystem.fss` is the compiled path's `System`. It is not in the compiled prelude: `WellKnownNames.useCompilerLibraries()` names `CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerBuiltin`, `CompilerAlgebra` and `AnyType`. 27 files in `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/` name it (counted 2026-10-28). At the switch-over, P-37 deletes the prelude's three files and keeps their tests. It does not name `CompilerSystem`, and no other entry does. His words speak of the compiler's second library as a whole: "the compiler second library is just a bootstrap and we need to get rid of it" (2026-09-20 14:39 UTC), and "We need to make the fortress use a single library." (2026-09-29 12:17 UTC). The phase 3 zero audit assumes that the one library's `System` takes its place. Is `CompilerSystem` deleted then, and do the tests that import it move to the one library's `System`?

**Does P-26 keep his reason, "learned what is feasible" (P-26)?** P-26 ranks the type group's later positions above the specification's early text. Its reason is his own: the early text was a wish, and the type group then worked to make the language run and learned what is feasible. On 2026-09-23 at 07:26 UTC he wrote: "The spec was written in a vacuum early on." and "And when that wish met reality, then the spec must change." The foundations judgement objects to this reason. A limit that the team met on the Java virtual machine tells how the team built Fortress. It is no reason to rank one language text above another. The judgement gives another reason. The type group's texts of 2011, 2012 and 2019 are later than the Working Draft and agree with each other, and the Working Draft contradicts itself. Keep his reason, or replace it with the judgement's?

- P-27 **Whoever extends the library follows the library's own practice.** What microGPT invented goes into the standard library, in the library's own style. Whoever extends the library first studies how it does the same kind of thing, and follows that pattern; exclusion, for one, is all over it. He had to find the diagonal's override himself (P-88) because that study was skipped. No fix is designed from the specification alone or from a workaround on the user's side. This rule governs how the library is extended. It does not choose between two of the team's designs of the language, such as the self type as the interpreter's library and the compiler's prelude write it: the team's later word, dated against the texts, decides between them (P-26).
- P-146 **In a self-typed trait, the compiled checker types `self` in the method bodies as also being the implementing type.** A self-typed trait is a trait `C[\X\]` whose parameter `X` extends `C[\X\]`, such as `Integral[\I extends Integral[\I\]\]`. In its method bodies, `self` has the type `C[\X\] & X`. The method signatures keep the plain trait type, because the proofs of the POPL 2019 paper on multiple dispatch (Park, Hong, Steele and Ryu) assume that no declared type holds a type parameter inside an intersection. Only the overloading check's exclusion test reads `self` in a signature as `C[\X\] & X` (P-157). The checker refuses a type that extends such a trait at another type, since an extender must be a subtype of the static argument that it gives: `object Bad extends Integral[\ZZ32\]` is refused, because `Bad` is not a `ZZ32`. Scala has the same rule for self types. The library's text gains no self type and no `comprises` clause, and walk is unchanged. The rule accepts every self-typed method body of the library except `Integral`'s `numerator`, which each integer type declares instead. Why: the team's later texts point, if weakly, toward the rule, and peer languages share it. The compiler's prelude writes the self type as a `comprises T` clause instead, and that form does not bind the library: Naden's write-up on the Return Type Rule (P-26 names it), later than the team's last edits of that clause, puts the self type in bounds only, the form `X extends C[\X\]` that the library writes. F-225 states the rule as built and holds the dates.
- P-153 **The integer power splits on the base: an integer base gives an integer or raises an error, and a float or rational base gives the fraction.** Each integer type's `^` returns its own type at every exponent. At a negative exponent, the bases 1 and -1 give their exact power, a base of 0 raises `DivisionByZero`, and any other base raises `IntegerOverflow`. A program that wants a fraction writes a float or rational base, as in `2.0^(-1)`. Why: the Working Draft's power, which gives a rational at a signed exponent, was never built on either path. The only power with an integer result type that the team built is the compiler's prelude's, which gives `ZZ32`, `NN32` and `NN64` each a power of its own type at every exponent. Overloads choose by type, and no type tells a negative exponent from a non-negative one, since a signed integer or a numeral can be either. So the split is on the base, and the sign of the exponent is tested at run time, as the library tests a value's sign everywhere (P-80, run-time sign tests in place of sign-refined types). Row 441: the same rule on the compiled path, whose own powers give 0 at a negative exponent and a raw Java exception at a base of 0, and overflow silently or with a raw Java exception (row 523).
- P-154 **A list is ordered only where its element type is totally ordered.** The library's `List` extends its lexicographic order only where its element type extends `StandardTotalOrder` (conditional extension, P-151). Floats and `QQ` are only partially ordered, since NaN, and `QQ`'s 0/0, compare with nothing. So on the compiled checker a list of floats or of `QQ` has no order: no `<`, `CMP` or the other comparisons, though its `=` stays. A pair of floats stays ordered: the curator accepted that mismatch as a cost of the list rule. The tuples' own rule is not decided here. No lexicographic trait over partially ordered elements is added now: the team never wrote one, and the case touches neither the distance to the switch-over nor microGPT. Why: the two lexicographic traits of an unfinished library draft of the team's (`Library/incomplete/advanced/Fortress.PartialTotalOrders.fss:117-140`) both bound the element by a total order, and conditional extension is a `where` form that the team wrote (P-151). The draft is not shown to be later than the specification's sentence that lets a list's order be partial where its elements' order is, so it does not count as the team's later word (P-26). Row 774: walk's half, since walk still gives every list an order.
- P-12 **After the switch-over, walk runs the compiled type checker on its programs, and then uses the static coercions that the checker inserts.** The curator wants the checker usable on the programs that walk runs. Today `fortress typecheck` checks a program only against the compiler's prelude, so it is no check of walk's programs (F-9 holds this fact). Walk is not changed for this before the switch-over. After it, walk runs the checker on its programs and so gains their static types. Walk then uses the static coercions that the checker inserts, in place of its choice on the run-time value (P-59, walk's choice of coercions until the switch-over). The step has three parts, and its size is unmeasured. First, walk must run with the Scala checker on; today it runs with it off. Second, walk must evaluate the `CoercionInvocation` nodes that the checker inserts, for which it has no case today (F-9 holds both facts). Third, the components that walk's programs import must be cleared of the checker's errors, each before this step or before the first program that needs it (F-290 counts them).
- P-17 **Unboxed doubles and arrays of unboxed doubles are required: without them the revival misses its point.** Why: a language meant for high performance cannot box its numbers. The specification states the same intent: its chapter on objects lets an implementation freely copy value objects, among them floating-point numbers, and its chapter on memory sequences makes a `LinearSequence` of a value type a sequence of "unboxed" values. Today the code generator boxes every number: an `RR64` value is an object of the class `FRR64`. In Java models of microGPT's three array kernels, the dot product, the matrix product and the row lift, boxing is the main cost (F-11 holds the measurement). How arrays store doubles, as `double[]`, is P-84's decision.

## After the new facts: the two pointers

Once F-293 and F-294 exist, P-37 and P-158 change once more (`facts-new.md`).

### P-37

A pointer to F-293, the compiler's fourth file `CompilerSystem`, is added in the parenthesis on the tests. It names the file and decides nothing. It answers finding P-37 d, which the sort puts in FACTS.

New:

> - P-37 **One library, the interpreter's, is the library that the compiler checks.** The interpreter's prelude, `FortressLibrary` and `FortressBuiltin`, becomes the compiled path's prelude in place of the compiler's own, and the compiled path reads the interpreter's library with it. Why: the switch-over exists to avoid the need to port the interpreter's library into the compiler's library; the revival is developing the type checker further, so that it will accept the fuller library that the interpreter uses. The curator sees the compiler's prelude, its own library files `CompilerLibrary`, `CompilerBuiltin` and `CompilerAlgebra`, as a bootstrap to remove. So no declaration is added to the compiler's prelude, and at the switch-over its three files are deleted and their tests kept (P-38 says which tests are respelled; F-293 holds the compiler's fourth file, `CompilerSystem`). The decision 

### P-158

The false sentence on the specification is replaced by a pointer to F-294, the export rule, which asks no declaration of an abstract member, and the false date "of 2012" is cut from the clause on the team's export check. It answers findings P-158 a and b, which the sort puts in FACTS and the history, each with a cut.

New:

> - P-158 **A member that an api writes `abstract` is declared in the component that exports the api.** The component's trait or object declares each such member at the api's header, with a body or without one. The compiled export check refuses a component that leaves one out, and the checker then checks that each object defines it. Why: the compiler's prelude, the team's later work, restates each such member in the component without a body, and the team's export check enforces it; that way wins over the interpreter's library, written earlier for walk, which leaves some out. The specification's export rule asks no declaration of an abstract member (F-294). Without the declaration, a compiled client's call of the member dies with `NoSuchMethodError` (row 816).

### The two new facts

> - F-293 **`CompilerSystem` is a fourth file of the compiler's library, outside its prelude, and compiled tests import it by name.** `Library/CompilerSystem.fsi` and `.fss` are the compiled path's own `System` api (`args`, `getProperty`). No program imports it by default: the compiled path's default imports are the prelude's three files and `AnyType` (`WellKnownNames.useCompilerLibraries`). 27 programs of `compiler_tests/` and one of `other_compiler_tests/` import it. P-37 names only the prelude's three files. Read in the tree. Detail: `reviews/phase3-exit/zero-audit.md`, "A.2 Scope".

> - F-294 **The specification's export rule asks a component to declare each field and non-abstract method of an api's trait or object, not its abstract methods.** The component's declaration has the api's header and may give an abstract method a body (`Specification/basic/components/source-code.tex`, "Export Statements"; `apis.tex` agrees). So P-158 asks more, and no revision note records it (P-95). The team's export check refused a missing abstract member from 2009 (row 816). Read in the source.
